title: Classical propositional sequents

based_on.title: Proof Theory: Foundations and Applications (June 2013 lecture notes)
based_on.pages: Sections 1.1–1.2, printed pp. 3–8, especially Exercise 4 and the invertible rules of Figure 1.2.

summary: Represent classical consequences by one-sided finite sequents, construct compound identities, and prove soundness of an atomic proof calculus.
abstract: A proof that an assumption implies a conclusion can be read as a proof that the assumption fails or the conclusion holds. One-sided sequents make these alternatives the objects of a proof calculus. We move negations to the atoms, then build finite proof trees using only opposite atom pairs, truth, conjunction, disjunction, and falsity. Identities for compound formulas follow from the atomic rule, and unused alternatives can be added without introducing a new primitive rule. Every resulting proof preserves Boolean truth. Explicit translations connect these sequents to ordinary propositional formulas, so a counterexample valuation still rules out a derivation.
